title: The Pangaea Architecture: Fault-Tolerant Heterogeneous Topological Codes via a Quantum Bus
authors: Sheir Yarkoni, Chen Scheim, Daniel Hakshuri, Nadav Katz
abstract: We introduce Pangaea, a fault-tolerant quantum architecture that uses a quantum bus to mediate logical operations between remote patches of two-dimensional topological codes. The bus is an auxiliary gauge-code strip whose measurements reconstruct joint logical operators while preserving nearest-neighbor physical connectivity. Enabling native heterogeneous topological codes and multi-qubit Pauli operations, the quantum bus can be interpreted as a three-dimensional generalization of lattice surgery. We require only $O(dN_L)$ physical qubits to implement multi-qubit interactions for $N_L$ distance-$d$ logical qubits, compared to $O(d^2N_L)$ of traditional two-dimensional architectures. At the 50-logical-qubit scale, Pangaea uses up to $10\times$ fewer physical qubits than planar surface-code architectures at matched logical error rates. We verify fault-tolerance of long-range measurement-based CNOT primitives for both surface--surface and surface--color joint parity measurements using pseudo-threshold simulations. We use this protocol to construct a native heterogeneous 15-to-1 magic-state distillation module using the quantum bus. These results establish Pangaea as a scalable architecture for three-dimensional fault-tolerant quantum computing that resolves the routing bottleneck of planar lattice surgery.
summary: The paper introduces Pangaea, a novel fault-tolerant architecture that uses a quantum bus to connect remote patches of heterogeneous topological quantum codes. This design overcomes the scaling limitations of planar lattice surgery by achieving superior qubit resource estimates for multi-qubit operations. It establishes a scalable pathway toward building large-scale, three-dimensional quantum computers.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a scalable, fault-tolerant quantum architecture to perform logical operations between remote patches of heterogeneous topological codes while overcoming the connectivity limitations of planar lattice surgery.
main_result: The proposed Pangaea architecture utilizes a quantum bus, achieving a significant scaling improvement by requiring only O(dN_L) physical qubits for multi-qubit interactions compared to O(d^2N_L) in traditional 2D setups. This allows for the construction of scalable, three-dimensional fault-tolerant quantum computing modules.
method: The method involves using an auxiliary gauge-code strip (the quantum bus) to mediate logical operations by reconstructing joint logical operators through carefully designed measurements, generalizing lattice surgery into a 3D process.
model_or_system: The system is the Pangaea architecture, which connects multiple patches of different topological codes (e.g., surface and color codes) via a quantum bus. This bus acts as an auxiliary gauge-code strip that facilitates long-range logical connectivity.
key_observables: Logical error rate ($p_L$), physical qubit count scaling ($O(dN_L)$ vs $O(d^2N_L)$), and the successful implementation of multi-qubit Pauli operations (e.g., CNOT, MZZ).
important_parameters: Distance ($d$) of the topological codes, number of logical qubits ($N_L$), and physical error rates ($p_{phys}$). The scaling factor improvement is quantified at the 50-logical-qubit scale.
main_assumptions: The architecture assumes that nearest-neighbor physical connectivity can be maintained throughout the process, simplifying construction compared to proposals requiring complex long-range physical links. It also relies on the ability to perform joint parity measurements across different code families.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the circuit-level stages of lattice surgery ('scissors' operator) using the bus for MZZ interactions; diagrams show 3D towers connecting non-adjacent qubits, and schematics detail surface-to-surface and surface-to-color patch connections via the bus.
paper_structure: The paper introduces Pangaea, detailing how the quantum bus mediates operations by reformulating lattice surgery. It mathematically derives the joint parity measurements required for long-range interactions, analyzes the scaling benefits over traditional methods, verifies fault tolerance through simulations, and discusses the resulting structure of merged heterogeneous codes.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it proposes a concrete hardware blueprint (the quantum bus) to overcome fundamental connectivity bottlenecks in implementing large-scale topological quantum error correction codes, which is central to building practical quantum computers.
